title: Reliability and quality of YouTube exercise videos for people living with lung cancer: a cross-sectional content analysis.
authors: Ergan M, Keskin T, Ünüvar BS et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the characteristics, reliability, and quality of YouTube exercise videos designed for people with lung cancer.
METHODS: Video characteristics (e.g., likes, views, video length, and upload source) were recorded. Information reliability was assessed using the mDISCERN scale, and overall quality was evaluated using the Global Quality Scale (GQS) and the JAMA benchmark criteria. Exercise-specific quality was additionally rated on a Likert scale focusing on exercise safety, progression/adaptability, and demonstration/instructions. Two physiotherapists independently analyzed the videos. Of 2,158 videos screened, 24 met the final eligibility criteria and were included in the analysis.
RESULTS: According to the GQS, 54.2% (n = 13) of the videos were classified as high quality and 20.8% (n = 5) as low quality. GQS scores were positively correlated with mDISCERN and JAMA scores, and mDISCERN scores were also positively correlated with JAMA scores (all p < 0.05). Exercise-quality parameters were not correlated with daily video views or likes (p > 0.05). Inter-rater agreement was high (Cohen's kappa: mDISCERN = 0.77, GQS = 0.72, JAMA = 0.68).
CONCLUSIONS: YouTube exercise videos for people with lung cancer show variable reliability and exercise-specific quality, with particular limitations in exercise demonstrations and instructions despite a substantial proportion being rated as high quality on the GQS.
IMPLICATIONS FOR CANCER SURVIVORS: YouTube provides readily accessible exercise information for lung cancer survivors; however, the reliability and quality of available videos vary, underscoring the need for guidance toward evidence-based resources.

title: Prognostic Value of Pretreatment Modified Glasgow Prognostic Score in Nivolumab-Treated Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Biter S, Kıdı MM, Aydınalp Camadan Y et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have become a standard treatment option for advanced/metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, considerable heterogeneity exists among patients regarding treatment response and survival. This study aimed to determine whether the pretreatment modified Glasgow Prognostic Score (mGPS), a marker of systemic inflammation and nutritional status, is prognostically associated with progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) in patients with advanced/metastatic NSCLC treated with nivolumab at a single tertiary oncology center. Methods: This retrospective, single-center cohort study included 130 adult patients with histologically confirmed advanced/metastatic NSCLC who received nivolumab at the Department of Medical Oncology, Çukurova University Faculty of Medicine. The pretreatment mGPS (0, 1, or 2), derived from baseline serum C-reactive protein (CRP) and albumin levels, was analyzed in relation to PFS and OS using the Kaplan-Meier method, log-rank test, and Cox proportional hazards regression. The prognostic value of mGPS was tested in multivariable Cox models adjusted for age, sex, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, histology, brain metastasis, liver metastasis, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR); the proportional hazards assumption was formally tested, and the incremental discriminative contribution of mGPS was assessed using bootstrap resampling. Results: Among 130 patients, 83.8% received nivolumab as second-line therapy. Pretreatment mGPS was 0, 1, and 2 in 40 (30.8%), 55 (42.3%), and 35 (26.9%) patients, respectively. Median OS was not reached, 9.7 months, and 3.0 months across mGPS 0, 1, and 2, respectively; corresponding median PFS values were 10.2, 4.8, and 3.0 months (log-rank p < 0.001 for both endpoints). After adjustment for age, sex, ECOG performance status, histology, brain metastasis, liver metastasis, and NLR, each one-point increase in mGPS remained associated with worse OS (adjusted HR 2.38; 95% CI 1.64-3.46; p < 0.001) and PFS (adjusted HR 1.81; 95% CI 1.32-2.48; p < 0.001), independent of the covariates included in the model. The proportional hazards assumption held for mGPS in both models. Addition of mGPS to the clinical-variables-only model was associated with higher model discrimination (Harrell's C-index: 0.676 to 0.737 for OS and 0.620 to 0.666 for PFS), a difference confirmed as statistically significant by bootstrap resampling (2000 iterations; 95% CI for the difference excluding zero, p < 0.001 for both endpoints). Conclusions: Pretreatment mGPS is a simple, readily available marker that shows a robust prognostic-rather than treatment-predictive-association with both OS and PFS in patients with advanced/metastatic NSCLC treated predominantly as second-line nivolumab monotherapy. Its addition to established clinical variables was associated with a statistically significant, though modest, improvement in prognostic discrimination. These findings require prospective, multicenter validation, including in first-line immunotherapy settings, before mGPS can be recommended for routine clinical risk stratification.

title: Cancer Stigma, Distress, and Cancer Coping in Relation to the Quality of Life Among Patients with Lung Cancer: A Cross-Sectional Study.
authors: Pyo JY, Yang S
abstract: Background/Objectives: Patients with lung cancer often experience impaired quality of life because of symptom burden and psychosocial difficulties. Cancer stigma and distress are associated with poorer quality of life, whereas adaptive coping may support psychological adjustment. This study examined the relationships among cancer stigma, distress, cancer coping, and quality of life and identified factors associated with quality of life in patients with lung cancer. Methods: This cross-sectional correlational study included 168 patients with lung cancer receiving inpatient or outpatient care at a university hospital in the Republic of Korea. Data were collected from 1 August to 1 September 2025, using structured self-report questionnaires. Descriptive statistics, group comparisons, Pearson correlations, and hierarchical multiple regression were performed. Results: The mean scores for cancer stigma, distress, cancer coping, and quality of life were 46.43 ± 8.46, 4.49 ± 2.53, 56.43 ± 15.07, and 74.02 ± 14.93, respectively; 57.1% of participants reported clinically significant distress. Quality of life was negatively correlated with cancer stigma (r = -0.63, p < 0.001) and distress (r = -0.76, p < 0.001) and positively correlated with cancer coping (r = 0.71, p < 0.001). Cancer coping, current activity level, and distress were independently associated with quality of life. The final model explained 75.2% of the variance, with cancer coping showing the largest standardized coefficient. Conclusions: Better cancer coping, higher activity levels, and lower distress were associated with better quality of life. Psychosocial nursing care should support adaptive coping, functional activity, and distress management.

title: [18F]F-AraG PET Imaging of Immunometabolic Activity in Individuals Without Malignancy.
authors: Chae HD, Nobashi TW, Shrestha U et al.
abstract: [18F]F-AraG is a clinical-stage PET tracer in immuno-oncology that accumulates in activated T cells and tissues with high mitochondrial biogenesis. Characterizing its distribution in individuals without malignancy is essential for interpreting immunometabolic states relevant to cancer biology. Methods: Twenty adults without active malignancy underwent a single [18F]F-AraG PET/CT scan, with tracer uptake assessed in relation to clinical history, medications, and demographic and physiologic factors. Results: Bilateral brown adipose tissue activation was identified in 3 participants receiving potentially brown adipose tissue-activating medications, in the absence of cold exposure or fasting. One showed elevated vertebral bone marrow uptake, previously linked to poor survival in immune checkpoint inhibitor-treated lung cancer. One of 2 participants with breast implants showed asymmetric periimplant uptake. Posterior pulmonary uptake occurred in a subset of participants, often with prior respiratory conditions and thoracic lymph node uptake. Conclusion: Whole-body [18F]F-AraG PET captures diverse immunometabolic activity in individuals without malignancy, reflecting systemic processes that may influence cancer and treatment outcomes.

title: Associations of in-hospital recovery, cancer self-management self-efficacy, and perceived social support with early return to work in young and middle-aged patients undergoing lung cancer surgery: a prospective cohort study.
authors: Yang J, Jiang L, Ge L et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Rehabilitation nursing plays a critical role in supporting postoperative functional recovery and facilitating reintegration into daily life and work, yet evidence on factors associated with early return to work (RTW) among young and middle-aged patients with lung cancer remains limited. This study aimed to examine the associations of in-hospital recovery, cancer self-management self-efficacy, and perceived social support with early RTW at 1 month after surgery among young and middle-aged patients with lung cancer.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study recruited 160 young and middle-aged adults who underwent minimally invasive lung cancer surgery at a tertiary hospital in Shanghai from June to December 2024. Before discharge, participants completed baseline assessments including the Quality of Recovery-15 scale, the Strategies Used by People to Promote Health, and the Perceived Social Support Scale. RTW status and RTW stage were assessed 1 month postoperatively. Binary logistic regression was used to examine factors associated with early RTW.
RESULTS: Among the 160 participants, 88 (55%) had returned to work 1 month after surgery, while 72 (45%) had not. Of those who returned to work, 53 were categorized into the "uncertain maintenance" stage and 35 into the "proactive maintenance" stage. Non-RTW participants were distributed across the "precontemplation" (n = 9), "contemplation" (n = 15), "prepared for action-self-evaluative" (n = 22), and "prepared for action-behavioural" (n = 26) stages. Higher levels of in-hospital recovery quality, self-efficacy, and perceived social support were significantly associated with an increased likelihood of early RTW.
CONCLUSION: More than half of young and middle-aged lung cancer patients resumed work within 1 month after surgery; however, most remained in the "uncertain maintenance" stage. Better postoperative recovery, higher cancer self-management self-efficacy, and stronger perceived social support were associated with a greater likelihood of RTW at 1 month after surgery in this population.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Therapeutic-scale CAR-NK microrobots with programmable swarm navigation for targeted solid tumor therapy.
authors: Wu Z, Wang Y, Zhang H et al.
abstract: An urgent requirement in chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) immune cell therapy [e.g., CAR-natural killer (NK) cells] for solid tumors is to engineer the cells for precise tumor targeting. Meanwhile, medical microrobots can be navigated toward specific target sites using external magnetic fields. Here, by bridging these approaches, we turn CAR-NK cells into magnetic biohybrid microrobots (CAR-NK microrobots) that achieve controllable long-distance targeted navigation at therapeutic doses (∼106 cells) in both murine and nonhuman primate animal models in vivo. CAR-NK microrobots are developed through genetic engineering with CAR structures and loading with magnetic nanoparticles for field-based navigation. Different magnetic field inputs reconfigure their swarms between vortex and ribbon modes, allowing dense aggregation for targeted navigation and further broad dispersion for large-area coverage. Using programmable magnetic fields, in vivo CAR-NK microrobot-based therapy is demonstrated for metastatic leptomeningeal carcinomatosis in brain's cerebrospinal fluid space. After intrathecal injection, the microrobots are magnetically guided long distance through the spinal canal toward the brain in vortex mode and subsequently spread over the target site in ribbon mode, as visualized by real-time angiographic imaging in a nonhuman primate model, providing a proof-of-feasibility demonstration in a nonhuman primate anatomical setting.

title: CTH Promotes Liver Cancer Progression and Exploratory Evaluation Supports Enhanced Antitumor Activity of PPG Plus GPC3 CAR-T Cells.
authors: Guo Y, Yu M, Zhu X et al.
abstract: Although hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a key regulator in cancer biology, the mechanism by which the H2S-producing enzyme cystathionine-γ-lyase (CTH) functions in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains elusive. Using the slow-releasing H2S donor GYY4137, we observed enhanced migration and invasion in HuH7 and HepG2 cells. Subsequently, we observed consistent protumorigenic effects of CTH not only in vitro but also in subcutaneous and orthotopic mouse models. Here, our findings suggest that CTH-H2S sulfhydrates Rab7a, which may be associated with HCC progression. We further showed that CTH modulates the expression of autophagy-related proteins in liver tumor cells. In nude mouse subcutaneous xenograft experiments, compared with the vehicle group, the combination of DL-propargylglycine (PPG, CTH inhibitor) and GPC3 CAR-T exhibited better antitumor efficacy compared to PPG or CAR-T alone. Our findings suggest that CTH modulation was associated with altered Rab7a sulfhydration and autophagy and that combined PPG and GPC3 CAR-T therapy exerts better antitumor efficacy.

title: Disrupted Signalling Landscapes in Glioblastoma: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Frontiers.
authors: Ansari AAA, Haddad N, Assed AM et al.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most prevalent and aggressive malignant primary brain tumour, originating from glial cells known as astrocytes and accounting for over 50% of all central nervous system malignancies. Its aetiology is linked to various factors, including radiation exposure, genetic alterations, and viral influences, which trigger the uncontrolled growth and rapid infiltration of glial cells into surrounding brain tissues. Despite standard multidisciplinary management involving maximal safe surgical resection, radiotherapy, and temozolomide, the prognosis remains poor. The molecular landscape of GBM is characterised by profound dysregulation across highly conserved signalling networks, including the PI3K/AKT/mTOR, ERK/MAPK, Wnt/β-catenin, and Hippo pathways. These pathways are frequently hijacked by genetic and epigenetic alterations such as EGFR amplification and PTEN loss, which drive essential hallmarks of cancer like uncontrolled proliferation, angiogenesis, and apoptosis evasion. A defining feature of GBM is its extreme intra-tumoral heterogeneity and cellular plasticity, where tumour cells dynamically transition between distinct transcriptional states, including mesenchymal, astrocyte-like, and neural progenitor-like, to adapt to therapeutic pressures. This complexity is further exacerbated by microenvironmental factors. Clinical progress is severely hindered by the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which restricts systemic agents from reaching invasive tumour margins. Targeted monotherapies, such as EGFR and mTOR inhibitors, have largely failed in clinical trials due to compensatory feedback loops and pathway redundancy. Consequently, the therapeutic paradigm is shifting toward rational combination therapies and novel immunotherapeutic platforms. Emerging strategies, such as bivalent CAR T-cell therapy targeting both EGFRvIII and IL-13Rα2, have shown early clinical promise in achieving tumour regression, highlighting a potential path toward precision medicine. This review synthesises current insights into signalling dysregulation and explores the future frontiers of multi-targeted therapeutic interventions in GBM.

title: Targeting SERPINB5 and MSLN for Pancreatic Cancer Therapy.
authors: Sun J, Liu L, Broadhurst R et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States and lacks efficient therapeutic options. Serine peptidase inhibitor, clade B, member 5 (SERPINB5) is non-inhibitory toward serine proteases, yet it has diverse biological functions, including regulating cell migration, cell death, gene expression, and stress responses. Mesothelin (MSLN) is a tumor-associated antigen that is broadly overexpressed on various malignant tumor cells and plays a crucial role in promoting proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. Methods: We integrated public database analyses, cell-line screening, gene knockdown and overexpression, immunoblotting, cell viability and apoptosis assays, flow cytometry, chromatin immunoprecipitation paired with quantitative PCR (ChIP-qPCR), and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy to investigate SERPINB5 and MSLN functions, developing a novel and effective therapeutic strategy for patients with pancreatic cancer. Results: Both SERPINB5 and MSLN are highly expressed and negatively associated with the overall survival of PC patients. Our mechanistic study suggests that SERPINB5 negatively regulates the mitochondrial protein dehydrogenase/reductase 2 (DHRS2) to promote PC cell survival; consequently, SERPINB5 depletion induces PC cell apoptosis. Of note, SERPINB5 depletion increases MSLN transcription by enhancing c-Myc binding to the MSLN promoter region, which in turn suppresses the mitochondrial protein DHRS2 and leads to resistance to apoptosis in PC cells. Our genetic ablation study shows that SERPINB5 and MSLN are critical for PC cell survival, and that depleting both proteins synergistically induces PC cell apoptosis. Gemcitabine (GEM) is a standard chemotherapy drug for PC treatment. Our study shows that SERPINB5-high PC cells display greater sensitivity to GEM than SERPINB5-low PC cells. GEM treatment increases mitochondrial DHRS2 protein expression, similar to the effect of SERPINB5 knockdown, whereas upregulated MSLN confers apoptotic resistance by decreasing DHRS2 levels. Conclusions: Our in vitro study demonstrates that sequential treatment with GEM followed by anti-MSLN chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells is an effective and promising strategy for patients with pancreatic cancer. Future studies using mouse models may validate the efficacy of this sequential treatment strategy in vivo.

title: Spatiotemporal multi-omics reveals lineage, spatial and functional heterogeneity of tumor-associated macrophages and therapeutic vulnerabilities in the tumor microenvironment.
authors: Wang T, Yang D, Wu J et al.
abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are central orchestrators of immune evasion, therapeutic resistance, and clinical outcome across diverse solid tumors. However, the classical M1/M2 paradigm fails to capture the lineage diversity, spatial heterogeneity, and functional plasticity of TAMs within the tumor microenvironment. Unlike previous reviews that mainly summarize macrophage polarization or TAM subtype classification, this review focuses on how emerging single-cell and spatial multi-omics technologies redefine TAM ontogeny, phenotypic diversity, spatial organization, and therapeutic vulnerabilities. This review summarizes how fate-mapping, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial multi-omics have contributed to the understanding of the dual origins of TAMs, including embryo-derived tissue-resident macrophages and monocyte-derived macrophages, and how these technologies further delineate transcriptionally and functionally distinct TAM subsets such as SPP1+, TREM2+, C1QC+, and MMP9+ TAMs with context-dependent roles in immune regulation, metastasis, and treatment resistance. We then integrate spatial transcriptomics, multiplex imaging, and radiomics evidence to outline TAM-enriched niches at hypoxic cores, invasive fronts, perivascular regions and tertiary lymphoid structures, emphasizing how these niches coordinate crosstalk among cancer cells, T cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, endothelial cells and B cells. Emerging TAM-related gene signatures and multi-omics-based scores were further highlighted that predict response or resistance to radiotherapy, chemotherapy, anti-angiogenic therapy, and immune checkpoint blockade. Finally, we provide a forward-looking perspective on strategies to reprogram, deplete, or redirect specific TAM subsets, including CSF1/CSF1R and CCR2/CCL2 blockade, metabolic and epigenetic modulators, agonists of phagocytosis, and CAR-macrophage-based therapies. Overall, we propose that integrating single-cell and spatial omics with AI-assisted digital pathology and longitudinal sampling will enable TAM-informed patient stratification and rational design of combination immunotherapies, thereby accelerating the translation of TAM biology into precision oncology.

title: Next-generation natural killer cell therapy: bench to bedside and beyond.
authors: Zhao A, Xu J, Deng W et al.
abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells have emerged as central players in cancer immunotherapy, progressing from basic discovery to clinically validated platforms over five decades. This review synthesizes the evolving understanding of NK cell biology, including subset heterogeneity, epigenetic regulation, and metabolic control, and, as innovative focal points, intratumoral NK heterogeneity, epigenetic modulation, and intracellular immune checkpoints, forming the foundation for rational therapeutic engineering. We examine the clinical trajectory from unmodified adoptive transfer to cytokine-induced memory-like NK cells and, most transformatively, to chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-NK cells. Landmark trials have established the remarkable efficacy and superior safety of CAR-NK cells in B-cell malignancies, with recent studies extending these benefits to autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and systemic sclerosis, demonstrating durable immune reset with a favorable safety profile. Despite these advances, solid tumors remain formidable challenges, hindered by antigen heterogeneity, physical barriers, and a metabolically hostile microenvironment. We therefore analyze next-generation engineering strategies that move beyond single modifications toward systems-level reprogramming, encompassing intrinsic enhancements (cytokine signaling, metabolic fitness, checkpoint disruption), extrinsic tumor microenvironment remodeling, and advanced delivery platforms. We further synthesize the practical dimensions of clinical translation by systematically examining key optimization parameters that will guide the path toward precision NK cell therapy. These include rational dosing and scheduling regimens, strategies to reduce lymphodepletion intensity, context-dependent persistence requirements across different disease indications and the emerging biomarker landscape.

title: Genomic correlates with survival after treatment of oesophageal adenocarcinoma by surgery alone
summary: New prognostic biomarkers for oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC) may help treatment planning as current staging does not accurately predict survival for many patients. We used a 451 cancer-associated gene panel to assess genomic alterations associated with survival for a cohort of 65 OAC patients who underwent surgical resection without perioperative treatment, reflecting institutional practice at the time. Median age at operation was 72 years, 88% were male, median 32 lymph nodes were removed per patient, and minimum follow-up exceeded 11 years. TNM stages (pTNM, 8th ed.) were 14% stage 1, 14% stage 2, 45% stage 3, and 6% stage 4 (non-locoregional nodal metastases). Copy number changes were common, and somatic mutations were similar to those reported previously. Genetic associations with worse survival included amplification of CCND1 (HR=3.08, p=0.02), EGFR (HR=2.98, p=0.01), loss of ARID2 (HR=2.12, p=0.05), KMT2D (HR=1.99, p=0.07) and missense mutation within RYR1 (HR=2.68, p=0.01). This study identifies candidate genomic prognostic biomarkers in OAC using a cohort treated by surgery alone, enabling assessment of tumour biology independent of the confounding effects of peri-operative systemic therapy and radiotherapy. Several of the identified alterations are potentially targetable, supporting further investigation of genomic profiling to refine prognostication and guide treatment selection.

title: Behavior-coupled single-cell transcriptomics reveals trafficking protein-dependent regulation of tumor cell migration
summary: Aggressive cellular migration underlies cancer invasion and metastatic dissemination, yet the molecular programs defining highly migratory tumor cell states remain poorly characterized. In head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), metastatic progression is associated with poor clinical outcome, motivating method developments that link migratory behavior to underlying mechanisms. Here, we present behavior-coupled single-cell sequencing (BC-seq), a live-cell imaging-guided transcriptomic platform that enables real-time identification, isolation, and profiling of individual cells based on migratory behavior. Applying BC-seq to 10 HPV-negative oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), the most common HNSCC subtype, we distinguished fast-migrating cells (FMCs) from slow-migrating cells (SMCs) and identified transcriptional programs associated with aggressive migration. Mechanistically, BC-seq uncovered cholesterol-regulated signaling pathways and associated trafficking proteins involving SREBP2, STARD4, Cavin1/3, and VEGFR2 that promotes actin cytoskeletal remodeling and cellular motility. Disruption of STARD4-mediated cholesterol trafficking or Cavin1/3-dependent VEGFR2 nuclear translocation significantly impaired cell migration, linking cholesterol metabolism to migratory machinery. We next examined whether molecular programs associated with aggressive migration are reflected in clinical outcomes. A 15-gene expression signature derived from FMCs predicted distant metastasis with 83.6% accuracy in an independent OSCC cohort, outperforming conventional clinicopathological risk stratification. Together, our study establishes BC-seq as an approach for integrating dynamic cellular behavior with single-cell transcriptomics to uncover mechanisms of aggressive migration and clinically relevant molecular signatures.

title: PINK1-mediated mitophagy supports lung cancer initiation and limits the efficacy of KRAS-targeted therapy.
authors: Gonçalves D, Guilbaud E, Di Mascio L et al.
abstract: Mitophagy, the selective degradation of mitochondria by lysosomes, is a major mitochondrial quality-control pathway, yet its role in lung cancer initiation and therapeutic response remains poorly understood. We investigated PINK1-dependent mitophagy in human lung adenocarcinoma and directly monitored mitophagy in vivo using mito-QC reporter mice during lung tumor development. We found that PINK1 activity and mitophagy are increased in human tumors and are activated from the earliest stages of tumorigenesis. Genetic inhibition of PINK1 impaired oncogenic transformation but had little impact once tumor cells were established, identifying mitophagy as a critical early adaptation during lung cancer initiation. PINK1 deficiency markedly enhanced the efficacy of KRAS-targeted therapy in vitro and in vivo. Together, our findings identify PINK1-dependent mitophagy as an early vulnerability in KRAS-driven lung cancer and provide a rationale for targeting mitophagy to improve the efficacy of KRAS-targeted therapies.

title: KRAS G12S Positive Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Mimicking KRAS G12C Positivity on the AmoyDx PCR Panel: A Case Report.
authors: Sakaguchi T, Ito K, Nishio M et al.
abstract: A false-positive KRAS G12C on a multi-PCR assay using the amplification refractory mutation system can potentially occur in cases harboring certain multi-nucleotide variants other than KRAS G12C. A 62-year-old man with a large left upper lobe tumor was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. A multi-PCR assay by the AmoyDx Pan Lung Cancer PCR panel showed positivity for KRAS G12C and KRAS G12A/G12V/G12R/G13C. However, next-generation sequencing revealed a KRAS variant of c.34_35delinsTC (p.G12S). KRAS G12S multi-nucleotide variants may lead to false-positive KRAS G12C results on the multi-PCR assay.

title: Integrated Molecular, Clinicopathological and Immune Profiling of Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: The MONREPOS Hellenic Cooperative Oncology Group (HeCOG) Study (HE_2TR/13).
authors: Efthymiadis K, Soteriou C, Kotoula V et al.
abstract: Integrated assessment of tumour genomics and immune biomarkers may improve prognostic stratification in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). We examined the distribution and prognostic relevance of somatic pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants (PVs), somatic copy-number alterations (SCNAs), programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression and tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) in a multicentre cohort. This retrospective, multicentre study included 367 unselected patients with histologically confirmed NSCLC treated at 19 centres in Greece between 2000 and 2020. Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed in 267 tumours; PD-L1 tumour proportion score (TPS) and haematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-based TIL density were evaluated in 298 and 352 tumours, respectively. Overall survival (OS) was assessed using Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox regression analyses. TP53 (53.6%) and KRAS (16.5%) were the most frequently detected genes with PVs; SCNAs were identified in 22.5% of sequenced tumours and were more frequent in squamous than non-squamous histology. In multivariable analysis (254 complete cases), TIL density ≥10% (hazard ratio [HR] 0.72, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.52-0.99; p = 0.042) and ≥2 mutated genes (HR 1.44, 95% CI 1.08-1.92; p = 0.014) were independently associated with OS. PIK3CA-containing copy-number gains were significantly enriched in squamous tumours with low TIL density (p = 0.024), while FGFR1-containing copy-number gains showed a similar but non-significant trend (p = 0.088). In the present retrospective study, co-mutation burden and TIL density provided complementary prognostic information beyond clinicopathological variables in NSCLC. The association between selected copy-number gains and an immune-poor squamous phenotype warrants prospective validation.

title: Dynamic remodeling of the KRAS interactome by direct RAS inhibitors with distinct mechanism of action reveals convergent responses.
authors: Yang Y, Liu T, Cho CY et al.
abstract: KRAS is mutated in 30% of all human cancers. Small molecule inhibitors targeting KRAS with distinct mechanisms-of-action and variable specificities have entered the clinic, but their full effect on the RAS signaling network remains unclear. Here, we described the impact of RAS inhibition on the KRAS interactome using Proximity-dependent Biotin Identification. Two inhibitors were used: panRAS-ON, which forms a ternary complex between cyclophilin and RAS in the GTP-bound state; panKRAS-off, which binds to the KRAS switch II pocket. RAS inhibitors were found to significantly alter 16.5% of proteins in proximity to KRAS. Despite their distinct modality, the KRAS inhibitors induced highly correlated changes in the KRAS interactomes. Among KRAS-proximal proteins, Afadin was highly affected by RAS inhibition. AFDN is a key regulator of cell motility, invasion, and metastasis. Analysis of AFDN phosphorylation revealed that AKT only partially modulates p-Ser1718, while KRAS inhibition sufficiently abolished EGF-mediated AFDN phosphorylation. Silencing AFDN in a KRAS-driven non-small cell lung cancer model abolished chemotaxis and disrupted directional migration in an EGF-driven wound healing model. We demonstrated that KRAS is a central node in regulating growth factor-induced cell migration, and that KRAS inhibition plays a broader role than MAPK-mediated cell proliferation and survival.

title: Pulmonary Carcinoid Tumors (Lung Carcinoids): Current Concepts in Diagnosis and Management.
authors: Chan DL, Uehara Y, Kobayashi K et al.
abstract: Pulmonary carcinoid tumors are rare lung neuroendocrine neoplasms with diverse clinical behavior, ranging from indolent localized disease to metastatic progression. Diagnosis relies on histopathology but may be supplemented by immunohistochemical markers such as Ki-67. Recent molecular and multi-omic studies reveal substantial heterogeneity, identifying molecularly defined subgroups and highly proliferative carcinoids with aggressive behavior. Management includes surgical resection for localized disease and systemic therapies for advanced cases, such as somatostatin analogs, targeted agents, peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, and chemotherapy. While emerging molecular classifications and biomarker-driven strategies hold significant promise, current management of advanced pulmonary carcinoids relies heavily on extrapolated data from mixed neuroendocrine cohorts, underscoring the urgent need for prospective thoracic-dedicated trials to validate these paradigms in clinical practice. Emerging biomarker-driven trial designs and integrated precision medicine approaches offer opportunities to optimize therapy and improve outcomes in this rare tumor type.

title: A Retrospective Study of the Efficacy and Safety of Chemoimmunotherapy in Elderly Patients with Extensive-Stage Small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Kobayashi M, Watanabe S, Hirose S et al.
abstract: Background/Objectives: We evaluated the efficacy and safety of first-line treatment with a programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor plus platinum-based chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone in patients aged ≥75 years with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC). Methods: We retrospectively analyzed the patients with ES-SCLC treated within the Niigata Lung Cancer Treatment Study Group between August 2019 and April 2024. Results: A total of 364 consecutive patients were enrolled. After excluding 21 patients who did not receive treatment or had ineligible histological types, 343 patients were included in the analysis. Of these, 132 were aged ≥75. Compared with chemotherapy alone, administering a PD-L1 inhibitor with chemotherapy significantly improved the median overall survival among elderly patients (13.6 vs. 8.4 months; hazard ratio, 0.543; p = 0.0277). The median progression-free and overall survivals were similar between the ≥75-year and <75-year groups treated with PD-L1 inhibitor plus chemotherapy (4.9 vs. 4.8 months; p = 0.7611 and 13.6 vs. 15 months; p = 0.732, respectively). Immune-related adverse events (irAE) of ≥grade 3 occurred in 4 and 12 patients (p = 0.7823), and non irAE of ≥grade 3 occurred in 47 and 103 patients (p = 0.5247) in the ≥75-years and <75-years subgroups, respectively. Conclusions: In this retrospective study, among patients aged ≥75 years with ES-SCLC, the addition of a PD-L1 inhibitor to platinum-based chemotherapy was associated with longer overall survival. Progression-free and overall survival outcomes were comparable between elderly and younger patients, with no clear age-related difference observed in the incidence of adverse events of ≥grade 3.

title: Toward Precision Imaging in Lung NET: A Clinically Oriented Framework Integrating Dual Tracer PET and Radiomics.
authors: La Salvia A, Rossi RE, Paravani P et al.
abstract: Background: Pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors (lung NETs) comprise a biologically heterogeneous group of neoplasms ranging from indolent typical carcinoids to more aggressive atypical carcinoids. Accurate characterization of tumor biology is essential for optimizing staging, prognostic stratification, and treatment selection. Beyond conventional cross-sectional imaging, functional imaging and emerging quantitative imaging techniques are progressively redefining the diagnostic pathway. Methods: We performed a comprehensive narrative review of the current evidence regarding conventional radiological imaging, somatostatin receptor (SSTR) PET/CT, 18F-FDG PET/CT, dual-tracer imaging, and radiomics in lung NETs, integrating recent international recommendations from ENETS, ESMO, AIOM, and other major societies. Results: Contrast-enhanced CT remains the cornerstone of anatomical staging, whereas 68Ga-labelled somatostatin analogue (SSA) PET/CT provides highly sensitive assessment of receptor expression and patient eligibility for somatostatin analogue therapy and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). Conversely, 18F-FDG PET/CT identifies metabolically active and biologically aggressive disease, particularly in atypical carcinoids and tumors showing dedifferentiation. Increasing evidence supports the complementary role of dual-tracer PET/CT for non-invasive characterization of tumor heterogeneity, prognostic stratification, and treatment planning. Radiomics further expands this paradigm by extracting quantitative imaging biomarkers that may improve histological prediction, recurrence risk assessment, and individualized management. Although promising, radiomics remains limited by methodological heterogeneity and the lack of prospective validation. Conclusions: The integration of conventional imaging, molecular imaging, and quantitative radiomics supports a shift from lesion detection toward biologically driven precision imaging. Future prospective multicenter studies incorporating imaging biomarkers, artificial intelligence, and clinical-pathological variables may further support personalized management of patients with lung NETs.

title: Tarlatamab in Small Cell Lung Cancer and Extrapulmonary Small Cell Carcinoma: A Single-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study of Routine-Practice Outcomes.
authors: Bangolo A, Zhang L, Zhao J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tarlatamab, a Delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3)-targeting bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE), has demonstrated significant efficacy in relapsed small cell lung cancer (SCLC) in clinical trials. However, real-world clinical outcomes and its efficacy in extrapulmonary small cell carcinoma (EPSCC) remain sparsely characterized.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, single-institution cohort study of 24 adult patients with moderately pretreated advanced SCLC (n = 19) or EPSCC (n = 5) who received standard-of-care tarlatamab. Endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and safety.
RESULTS: Patients had received a median of two prior lines of therapy, and 38% had baseline brain metastases. The overall intent-to-treat (ITT) ORR was 25.0%. Among response-evaluable patients (n = 18), the ORR was 33.3%. Efficacy was notably discordant between histologies: the SCLC cohort achieved an ITT ORR of 31.6% (46.2% in evaluable patients), whereas 100% of EPSCC patients experienced progressive disease. Systemic responses were observed in patients with baseline brain metastases (ORR 33.3%). The safety profile was manageable; any-grade CRS and ICANS occurred in 58% and 29% of patients, respectively. Severe (Grade ≥ 3) toxicities were rare, and tocilizumab was utilized therapeutically in 50% of patients for low-grade toxicity.
CONCLUSIONS: These real-world data are consistent with tarlatamab's systemic efficacy and tolerability in SCLC. The lack of clinical benefit observed in this small EPSCC cohort raises a hypothesis that requires prospective biomarker-correlated evaluation.
